findings.where: Article specimen, body text: the two opening paragraphs, the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?', its intro line, the three-item numbered list and the closing paragraph. Desktop and phone.
findings.fault: The article's running text is centred. Every line starts at a different place, so long paragraphs are tiring to read. In the list it is worse: each item's text is centred while its number stays at the left, so item 2's and item 3's first words float far from their numbers and the items' wrapped lines start at different places.
findings.who_objects: Mark's readers at the development banks, who come for the articles (the research calls the article page 'the product'). They read long legal-policy prose, and centred paragraphs and a list whose numbers come loose from their text make it slow to follow. Angélique would also see every list she adds come out ragged.

findings.where: Section labels down the specimen: 'PALETTE', 'Type pair', 'Texture', 'An article page', 'Motion sketch'
findings.fault: The same kind of label is set four ways. 'PALETTE' is blue, letter-spaced capitals. 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' are small bold sans in sentence case. 'Texture' is a large italic serif heading. The page's own type note says 'Sentence case, never tracked capitals', and its colour note keeps blue for things you can click, yet 'PALETTE' breaks both. 'Texture' is also the only italic display line on the page.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging whether this tile's type system holds together. And Angélique, who needs one label style to copy, and here can't tell which of the four is the rule.

findings.where: Subscribe band under the hero, 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform', worst on phone
findings.fault: The band's heading is set in the same display serif at almost the size of Mark's line, and on phone it is about the same size or bigger. So the page's first view has two competing large serif lines, not one. The second is a third-person sales line, and it matches the hero's weight in type.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief asks for one very large serif line first and one message on the first screen. And a bank visitor scrolling on a phone, for whom the subscribe pitch looks as important as Mark's own words.

findings.where: Article specimen, the headline 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' and the byline 'Mark M. Moseley · Blog No. 8 · 18 September 2024'. Desktop and phone.
findings.fault: The byline sits right under the headline's descenders, almost touching, then there is a wide gap before the first paragraph. The byline reads as stuck to the headline, not as its own line, and the spacing is the opposite of the even rhythm the specimen's note promises.
findings.who_objects: A reader of the article page, who gets a cramped title block. And Angélique, whose posts will all copy this block.

findings.where: Footer name 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the address, against the nav name at the top of the hero
findings.fault: Mark's name is set in the serif at the top of the page and in the sans in the footer, so the same name is styled two different ways.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who wants Mark's name to lead as a consistent identity. A name set in two faces reads less like a signature.

findings.where: Palette section, the text-pair table on phone: the ratio '11.66 : 1' and the pair names ('warm / white on slate')
findings.fault: On phone the ratio breaks across lines, with '11.66 :' on one line and '1' on the next. The pair names wrap under their 'Aa' chips, so the label starts beside the chip and carries on below it.
findings.who_objects: The founder or a reviewer reading the specimen on a phone, who finds the ratio broken apart and the rows untidy.
